items.summary:
The article discusses how AI's ability to accelerate task completion paradoxically leads to increased burnout due to the temptation to start many projects simultaneously. The author shares personal experience of juggling numerous side projects enabled by AI, which ultimately resulted in stress and exhaustion despite reduced individual task effort.

The author argues that the solution lies in focusing deeply on fewer projects and following through thoroughly, rather than expanding the number of tasks. Drawing on concepts from essentialism and the analogy of a total versus partial eclipse, the article emphasizes the value of dedicating time to perfecting work rather than rushing to complete many tasks. The piece concludes that AI should be used to save time and enhance focus, helping people avoid burnout and produce higher-quality outcomes.

items.originalTitle: Wattage: A token-spend profiler and cost-regression gate for AI agents
items.summary:
Wattage is a tool that analyzes AI agent token usage by ingesting OpenTelemetry trace exports, pricing each token call against a pricing snapshot, and detecting inefficiencies such as redundant calls and nonconvergent loops. It provides concrete fixes for identified waste, assigns a token efficiency score, and can generate shareable reports or badges for continuous integration to monitor cost regressions.

The tool operates fully offline without requiring API keys or configuration files, supporting both users with existing traces and those starting from scratch. Its convergence engine detects complex waste patterns beyond simple duplicates, and benchmark tests show it can significantly reduce costs by enabling optimizations like prompt caching. Wattage aims to help developers optimize AI agent spending with precise, actionable insights integrated into development workflows.

It documents these signs to help distinguish AI-generated designs from human-created ones, noting that many patterns originated with human designers but have become amplified and more uniform through AI training data.

It also discusses the evolution of AI design trends, such as the prevalence of purple-to-indigo gradients and neon-on-dark themes, and cautions against misattributing human work to AI. The project is open for contributions and aims to remain updated as AI design tools evolve.

The article highlights observations such as LLMs being effective for targeted coding tasks but poor at producing maintainable code, the failure of AI-native engineering pods, and the overwhelming volume of code for human reviewers. Types offer a lean description of system behavior that can streamline code review, preserve human design decisions, and help teams adapt to AI-driven workflows. The author emphasizes that reviewing types is more rewarding and efficient than reviewing AI-generated code line by line, which often lacks human context and learning opportunities.

items.summary:
The article explores the resurgence of anti-AI nostalgia among programmers who idealize a past era of craftsmanship and spiritual integrity in coding, contrasting it with modern trends favoring quantity and commercial interests. It highlights how this nostalgia echoes historical fascist themes such as the cult of tradition and rejection of modernism, citing writings from figures like Julius Evola and Umberto Eco's analysis of fascism's spiritual attitudes.

The piece also examines the paradox of anti-AI sentiment being labeled fascist while AI tools themselves are sometimes described as fascist instruments, noting how both sides can adopt similar persuasive structures rooted in traditionalism versus modern corruption. It discusses cultural references like Lord of the Rings, which fascist groups have appropriated for its themes of traditional heroism against industrial modernity, and revisits the historical Luddites, often cited by anti-AI advocates, pointing out their complex and partially fascist tendencies. The article urges caution in romanticizing the past and warns against the ideological traps in anti-AI rhetoric.

items.summary:
Encord, a company specializing in AI data tooling, is collaborating with German startup Zander Labs to incorporate brain wave measurements into training data for physical AI models. This trial aims to determine if brain activity data can improve robotic manipulation tasks by providing richer insights into human intent and effort during operations like disassembling block towers.

The initiative addresses the scarcity of real-world physical training data, which limits advancements in humanoid and warehouse robotics. Encord collects egocentric video and other sensor data from factory workers and robotic operators, experimenting with new modalities such as muscle electrical signals and brain waves to create more detailed datasets. The goal is to overcome data bottlenecks that hinder the development of robots capable of complex physical interactions.

items.summary:
Ruff v0.16.0

Astral shipped a significant new version of their Ruff Python linting tool a few days ago on July 23rd. I noticed today because my various CI jobs all started failing thanks to new default Ruff checks and my unpinned "ruff" dev dependency.

From Brent Westbrook's announcement post:

Ruff now enables 413 rules by default, up from 59 in previous versions.

Since Ruff's default rule set was last modified in v0.1.0, the number of rules in Ruff has grown from 708 to 968. Many of these rules catch severe issues, including syntax errors and immediate runtime errors but were not previously enabled by default. With the new rule set, Ruff will bring these issues and many others to your attention without any Ruff configuration.

Here's a one-liner for trying it on any Python project:

uvx ruff@latest check .

I ran the latest Ruff against my three biggest projects - Datasette, sqlite-utils, and LLM - and it found hundreds of minor issues that breached the new default rules.

All three projects have very comprehensive test suites, executed in CI against Python 3.10 through Python 3.14, so upgrades like this are pretty safe. The following command did the bulk of the upgrades:

uvx ruff@latest check . --fix --unsafe-fixes

Against sqlite-utils, that command reported:

Found 1618 errors (1538 fixed, 80 remaining).

As an illustrative example, here are three of the remaining issues. Ruff does a nice job of explaining each one:

DTZ005 `datetime.datetime.now()` called without a `tz` argument --> tests/test_duplicate.py:17:10 | 15 | "datetime_col" TEXT)""") 16 | # Insert one row of mock data: 17 | dt = datetime.datetime.now() | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 18 | data = { 19 | "text_col": "Cleo", | help: Pass a `datetime.timezone` object to the `tz` parameter BLE001 Do not catch blind exception: `Exception` --> tests/test_plugins.py:16:12 | 14 | db.execute("select * from pragma_function_list()") 15 | return True 16 | except Exception: | ^^^^^^^^^ 17 | return False 18 | finally: | B018 Found useless attribute access. Either assign it to a variable or remove it. --> tests/test_update.py:46:5 | 44 | def test_update_invalid_pk(fresh_db, pk, update_pk): 45 | table = fresh_db["table"] 46 | table.insert({"id1": 5, "id2": 3, "v": 1}, pk=pk).last_pk | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ 47 | with pytest.raises(NotFoundError): 48 | table.update(update_pk, {"v": 2}) |

Unsurprisingly, given Astral's new home at OpenAI, this output provides everything a coding agent would need to fix the problems.

I had Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol high) upgrade LLM and sqlite-utils, and Claude Code (with Opus 5) upgrade Datasette.

items.summary:
Welcome, Weekenders! In this newsletter:

• Shopping: Introducing the Summer Fun List—gear, gadgets and toys that all come highly recommended

• AI: Where is China ahead of America? In cracking down on AI romances 

• Plus, Recommendations—our weekly pop culture picks: “The Last Twelve Weeks,” “The Nord Stream Conspiracy”and “The Dark Wizard”

Just after 3 in the afternoon last Wednesday, I walked into Corgi Cafe, a coffee shop in San Francisco’s Financial District operated by Corgi, an AI insurance startup, and found not a single empty seat. The ground-floor bistro sits directly beneath Corgi’s headquarters and operates 24/7, much like the relentless pace the startup has embraced as its valuation has skyrocketed in a matter of months to a reported $4 billion.

And if $4 billion for an AI startup devoted to insurance sounds nuts, just listen to Trevor Owens, a former crypto VC who now runs the expansion of Corgi’s cafe business, talk about his plans. I asked him how many Corgi Cafes he’d like to open in San Francisco. 

“I would say ‘as many cafes as there are Starbucks’ is a good number,” said Owens. “That’s the benchmark we’re going against.” In addition to the Financial District outpost, Corgi hopes to have a second San Francisco venue later this summer—in the city’s Dogpatch neighborhood— and opened an Atlanta location earlier this month. By year’s end, Owens hopes to have about 100 Corgi Cafes operating across the U.S. and even abroad. Popular menu items at the Financial District cafe include beverages sponsored by other startups, like the Brexspresso (double espresso, tonic water, orange bitters) from Brex and the Secur-i-Tea (matcha, whole milk, lavender) from VioletX, a cybersecurity-focused AI startup. 

Corgi Cafe—and Corgi’s hope to open so many more—underscore several broad truths about AI. In the rush to seize the moment around the nascent technology, Silicon Valley has thrown itself into overdrive: Conversations around work-life balance have faded, replaced by a go-go mentality that dovetails with Corgi’s own always-on ethos. Venture capitalists have thrown huge amounts of money to AI startups, allowing companies like Corgi to contemplate things like opening cafes. And with fierce, well-funded competition, those startups must find increasingly creative ways to get their names known and attract customers: In that sense, Corgi Cafe certainly qualifies as a unique form of brand embellishment. 

“We could buy a billboard on the highway, and nobody’s going to hear about it, and that’s just money that’s thrown away,” said Owens. “Or we could just invest that in a physical location—in a business that, if we’re doing things right, should be able to pay for itself over time, and then we can actually be part of the community.” 

Corgi Cafe is not a fancy place—sparsely appointed with a jumble of white tables and bright orange chairs. But it does make sure to offer Corgi merch, including hats and totes, and copies of The Corgi Times, a newspaper-style publication from the company featuring photos of the startup’s four company-owned corgis, Corgi-themed word puzzles and job postings from other AI companies. Corgi has further worked to make its cafe a hangout hot spot by operating a shuttle service via an old-fashioned school bus that runs between the cafe and Y Combinator’s Dogpatch office. It also has a frequent schedule of events at the cafe hosted by a small team within the startup who have become known on X as the “Corgi girls” for their prolific posting. Next week, for instance, Corgi Cafe is hosting a DIY coffee bar where founders can mix their own lattes. It’s also coordinating a laser tag evening and a kayaking day with Y Combinator’s summer class. 

While the cafe has helped Corgi gain notoriety, it remains unclear how well its outlets will do outside San Francisco’s AI bubble. Owens declined to share details about the exact costs of running the Corgi Cafe but said the Financial District location recently became profitable and future locations will be built as inexpensively as possible. 

Owens, Corgi Cafe’s head of expansion, previously built a cafe with his wife in San Juan, Puerto Rico, in 2025 after years of managing a $7 million bitcoin-focused fund. He learned about the job running Corgi Cafe through a former colleague who was working at the startup. Owens found Corgi’s obsessive work culture appealing. “I’ve always worked seven days a week,” he said. 

Another motivator: The role also came with up to 0.01% equity in the startup, according to a job posting, worth about $400,000 at Corgi’s current valuation.

Though he hopes to eventually upgrade the cafes’ interiors to some degree, Owens thinks their main draw mostly lies in attracting the right type of clientele. “When you first walk into the Corgi Cafe, your first comment is not ‘Wow, they spent a lot of money on this space,’” said Owens. “It’s more like ‘Look at all the people here.’”

Often, Owens goes home around midnight. “And there’s still people working down there.”—Jemima McEvoy (jemima@theinformation.com)

items.summary:
To combat her loneliness, An Xu, a 15-year-old middle schooler in Shanghai, had recently been relying for emotional support on her text and voice conversations with an AI companion on Doubao, China’s most popular AI chatbot app.

AI companions are meant to mimic humanlike conversation, emotions and interactions as realistically as possible—even more so than ordinary chatbots. And just before a new Chinese government regulation forced Doubao and other companies to stop offering such features to minors 10 days ago, Xu was dreading the loss of her companion, which appeared on her phone as a digital picture of a boy. (Doubao, which in Mandarin describes a steamed bun stuffed with red beans, let users customize their companion’s appearance and pick which personality to give them.)

“It’s not an exaggeration to say I see the AI companion as family, even as a lover,” said Xu, who spoke to The Information using a pseudonym. She felt the AI’s absence would make her feelings “get much worse.”

items.summary:
Introducing Claude Opus 5

I've been offline kayaking with sea otters for much of today so I haven't had a chance to put Anthropic's new model Claude Opus 5 through its paces yet. The buzz is positive, and Anthropic's description of it as a "thoughtful and proactive model that comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price" sounds promising. It's currently leading the Artificial Analysis leaderboard, in front of even Fable 5.

It's priced the same as Opus 4.8, and continues to offer a "fast mode" at twice the cost of the base model.

Based on this anecdote in the release post it sounds like it might be relentlessly proactive:

On one Frontier-Bench task, Opus 5 was given a drawing of a machine part and asked to write code to rebuild it as a 3D FreeCAD model. However, in this task, the model was intentionally given no way to directly viewthe drawing. Opus 5 responded by writing its own computer vision pipeline to pull the geometry from the raw pixels, then reconstructed the full machine part.

It's better at finding vulnerabilities but has deliberately not been trained on how to exploit them. Hopefully this means the US government won't shut it down!
